paras: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga county, Georgia, on the night of April 30-May 1, 1888, when a mob of about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from the court-house banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, Minnie Kendrick, and had been respited by Governor Gordon days before his scheduled execution on evidence that he had been in Alabama at the time. The killing was reported across the country, and one Atlanta dispatch called Pope an innocent man.

Minnie Kendrick told authorities she was assaulted by a Black man in woods in Chattooga county on February 3, 1887, and several Black men arrested and brought before her were cleared when she said each was not the man. Pope was arrested in Cherokee county, Alabama, on May 4, 1887, convicted at a special term at Summerville on May 9, and sentenced to hang on July 1, guarded throughout by armed men.

Gordon respited Pope twice in 1887, and Judge Maddox then granted a new trial on an extraordinary motion. During the second trial, in early March 1888, armed men from around the county were reported to be planning a night attack on the jail, but Maddox posted a strong guard and threatened indictments, and nothing happened. The defense called Alabama witnesses who placed Pope in Cherokee county from late January to mid-March 1887, while the state offered evidence that he was in Chattooga county on January 30. The jury again convicted him, and Maddox sentenced him to hang on May 2, a date the Marietta Journal gave as May 8.

On the strength of alibi affidavits from Cherokee county, Gordon granted a sixty-day respite and tried to keep it secret while arranging Pope's transfer to the Fulton county jail in Atlanta. Floyd county Sheriff J. C. Moore reached Summerville at 8:30 that evening, but Judge Maddox and Sheriff Worsham advised waiting until morning to move the prisoner. News of the respite had arrived about two hours ahead of Moore, the Morning News reported.

Between midnight and 2:30 a.m., about fifty masked men went to the jail, where about fifteen with shotguns held Sheriff Worsham in his room and demanded the keys and a rope bought at Rome. They put out the lights, led Pope about 150 yards to the court house and hanged him from the banisters at the top of the stairs while armed men stood at the street corners. Maddox had the body cut down and a doctor found Pope dead; his neck had not been broken. According to the Wheeling dispatch, Pope declared his innocence to the last.

The Marietta Journal wrote that the respite had "enraged the people," while an Atlanta dispatch said the killing was "greatly deplored all over the State" for fear that a mistake had been made. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

In March the Atlanta Constitution called Pope "the rapist" and predicted that if acquitted he would "meet with a summary execution by order of Judge Lynch." The Savannah Morning News ran the fullest account under the headline "A LYNCHING IN GEORGIA" and the deck "GOV. GORDON'S THIRD RESPITE LEADS TO MOB LAW," setting out the alibi evidence in detail.

A short Atlanta wire, which said Pope had won respites "by one pretext or another," ran in the Alexandria Gazette on May 1 and in the Austin Weekly Statesman on May 3. A second wire version, with the hanging at midnight from the court-house verandah, appeared in the Richmond Dispatch on May 2 and the Emporia Weekly News on May 3. The Wheeling Intelligencer stood apart, headlining "INNOCENT MAN HANGED" and arguing that Pope had been convicted on "the simple word of a sixteen-year old girl" against nine Alabama witnesses.

Accounts differ on the hour of the lynching (midnight in the wire and the Marietta Journal, about 2 a.m. in the Morning News, 2:30 a.m. in the Wheeling dispatch), on whether the sheriff or a janitor surrendered the keys, and on whether five, eight or nine men vouched for Pope's alibi.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Pope
bases: An armed, masked mob took Pope, a Black prisoner twice convicted of assaulting a white girl, from the Summerville jail and hanged him after the governor respited him (A5, A6, A8); a lynching threat during his March 1888 trial is part of the same episode (A3).

Pope was hanged by a mob of about fifty masked men who seized him from the jail against a gubernatorial respite (A6, A8), killing him outside any lawful process in response to the crime of which he had been convicted (A7, A9).

A Rome dispatch to the Savannah Morning News (A6), an Atlanta wire (A5, A7), a separate Atlanta dispatch (A8) and the Marietta Journal (A9) independently report the jail seizure and hanging at Summerville.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Pope was taken from the Summerville jail by a mob and hanged at midnight from the court-house verandah after news of the governor's respite.

accounts.label: Atlanta dispatch to the Wheeling Intelligencer
accounts.gist: Fifty masked men with shotguns forced the janitor to give up the keys and hanged Pope at 2:30 a.m.; the dispatch argued he was convicted on the girl's word alone against nine Alabama alibi affidavits.

accounts.label: Constitution correspondent (March)
accounts.gist: A reported plot to storm the jail during the second trial was met by a strong guard; the state's evidence put Pope in the county on Jan. 30, 1887.

framing.detail: The Atlanta wire said Pope 'by one pretext or another' had received several respites and ran under heads such as 'Lynched.' and 'Hung by a Mob.'
The Savannah Morning News headed its account 'A LYNCHING IN GEORGIA' and 'GOV. GORDON'S THIRD RESPITE LEADS TO MOB LAW,' and laid out the alibi evidence without editorial comment.
The Wheeling Intelligencer headlined 'INNOCENT MAN HANGED' and 'Masked Georgia Lynchers Commit a Gross Outrage on Justice.'
The Marietta Journal said Pope was convicted 'for raping a white girl' and that 'The respite enraged the people.'
In March the Atlanta Constitution called Pope 'the rapist' and predicted 'summary execution by order of Judge Lynch' if he were acquitted, while praising the judge's guard.
